results.authors: Mas JL, Derumeaux G, Guillon B, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients aged 16 to 60 with a recent stroke attributed to a PFO with an atrial septal aneurysm or a large shunt, closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduced recurrent stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy alone over a mean follow-up of 5.3 years.
results.title: Patent foramen ovale closure or anticoagulation vs. antiplatelets after stroke (CLOSE)

results.authors: Saver JL, Carroll JD, Thaler DE, et al.
results.key_finding: In the extended follow-up of RESPECT, PFO closure reduced recurrent ischaemic stroke compared with medical therapy (hazard ratio 0.55), with a larger reduction for recurrent stroke of undetermined mechanism (hazard ratio 0.38).
results.title: Long-term outcomes of patent foramen ovale closure or medical therapy after stroke

results.authors: Messe SR, Gronseth GS, Kent DM, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients younger than 60 with a PFO and an embolic-appearing infarct and no other mechanism after a thorough evaluation, clinicians may recommend closure after discussing the absolute reduction in recurrent stroke and the procedural risks, including atrial fibrillation.
results.title: Practice advisory update summary: patent foramen ovale and secondary stroke prevention

output.summary: Randomized trials (CLOSE, RESPECT, REDUCE) support PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy over antiplatelet therapy alone in selected patients up to 60 years with an embolic-appearing stroke and no other mechanism, with the greatest benefit when the shunt is large or an atrial septal aneurysm is present. The RoPE score estimates the probability that a PFO is causal from age, vascular risk factors and a cortical infarct.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis or take the patient to thrombectomy: last known well is about 24 hours before arrival, the infarct already shows hemorrhagic transformation, and there is no occlusion.

Do not attribute the stroke to the vaccine or order anti-PF4 (VITT) testing after an inactivated vaccine with normal platelets and D-dimer: a temporal association is not causation, and the work-up shows a PFO with a large shunt.
Do not start anticoagulation in the acute phase of this infarct with hemorrhagic transformation without a venous thrombosis or thrombophilia to treat.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (before the left arm and leg numbness began at work the previous day, about 24 hours before arrival; the numbness persisted overnight, so finding him hemiplegic on waking does not reset it) and the NIHSS (16: LOC questions 1, gaze 1, facial palsy 2, left arm 4, left leg 4, sensory 2, dysarthria 1, extinction 1).

IV thrombolysis: do not give. Last known well is about 24 hours before arrival, far beyond 4.5 hours; this is not an unknown-onset stroke eligible for imaging selection (the deficit began the previous day and FLAIR is already positive); and MRI shows petechial hemorrhagic transformation (HI-1) before any treatment. Thrombectomy: not indicated, because CTA and MRA show no arterial occlusion.

Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours, a swallow screen before oral intake, intermittent pneumatic compression of the legs for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and early physiotherapy and occupational therapy for the left hemiplegia.

Start aspirin now (160 to 325 mg, then 75 to 100 mg daily); petechial (HI-1) transformation does not preclude it. Dual antiplatelet therapy is not indicated (NIHSS 16, not a minor stroke), and anticoagulation is not indicated without a venous thrombosis or thrombophilia.

VITT needs no testing here: it follows adenoviral vector vaccines 5 to 30 days after vaccination with thrombocytopenia and a markedly raised D-dimer, whereas this vaccine was inactivated, the interval was 24 to 48 hours, and platelets (224 x10^9/L) and D-dimer (250 µg/L) are normal. Report the temporal association to the national vaccine adverse-event reporting system.
If inpatient monitoring finds no atrial fibrillation, arrange prolonged ambulatory rhythm monitoring (30-day event monitor or implantable loop recorder) after discharge, before PFO closure.

Discuss percutaneous PFO closure with cardiology after the acute phase: age 36, an embolic-appearing territorial infarct with no other mechanism after full evaluation (normal vessels and venography, no atrial fibrillation so far, negative thrombophilia screen), RoPE score 9 and a large shunt (AAN 2020 practice advisory supports offering closure after shared decision-making; CLOSE, RESPECT, REDUCE).

Start atorvastatin 80 mg daily: LDL 112 mg/dL after a non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke without known coronary disease meets the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention indication (COR 1, SPARCL), although the mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO rather than atherosclerosis; target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

key_clinical_evidence: Left arm and leg numbness began at work about 24 hours before arrival and persisted overnight; he woke with dense left hemiplegia. Last known well is therefore about 24 hours before arrival, not the time he was found.

NIHSS 16 (LOC questions 1, gaze 1, facial palsy 2, left arm 4, left leg 4, sensory 2, dysarthria 1, extinction 1) and GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). The facial weakness is of upper motor neuron type, as expected from a hemispheric lesion, and gaze prefers the side of the lesion.
No reperfusion therapy: last known well about 24 hours, FLAIR already positive, petechial hemorrhagic transformation (HI-1) before treatment, and no occlusion on CTA or MRA.

The infarct conforms to the right MCA territory (cortical and lenticulostriate branches) with no persisting occlusion, the pattern of an embolus that has recanalized. MR venography is normal and D-dimer is 250 µg/L, so a venous infarct is set aside.

VITT is excluded on three independent grounds: an inactivated vaccine (VITT follows adenoviral vector vaccines), an interval of 24 to 48 hours rather than 5 to 30 days, and a normal platelet count and D-dimer.

Echocardiography with agitated saline shows a PFO with a large right-to-left shunt and no atrial septal aneurysm; vessels, venography, rhythm monitoring and the thrombophilia screen are normal, so the stroke is attributed to paradoxical embolism through the PFO.
RoPE score 9 (age 30 to 39: 4; no hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke or smoking: 4; cortical infarct: 1): the PFO is probably causal, and with a large shunt closure should be discussed (AAN 2020).

clinical_pearls: VITT requires thrombocytopenia and positive anti-PF4 antibodies — do not diagnose it based on temporal association with vaccination alone
Inactivated virus vaccines (Sinopharm, Sinovac) have not been associated with VITT, which is linked to adenoviral vector vaccines
PFO should be suspected in any young cryptogenic stroke patient, especially when vascular imaging is normal — always request a bubble study
Post-vaccination inflammatory state may contribute to a transient prothrombotic milieu, but this alone does not establish causation for stroke
The RoPE score helps quantify the probability that a PFO is stroke-related rather than incidental
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — young patient with no traditional risk factors presenting with acute ischemic stroke 24 hours after COVID-19 vaccination. The temporal association creates a strong cognitive anchor toward VITT, but normal platelets and coagulation exclude this diagnosis. The true mechanism (paradoxical embolism through PFO) is only revealed through systematic workup including echocardiography with bubble study. Multiple red herrings including vaccination timing, mildly elevated inflammatory markers, and hemorrhagic transformation complicate the diagnostic reasoning.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Young cryptogenic stroke with recent vaccine temporal association — comprehensive cryptogenic workup including PFO with bubble study, MRV, hypercoagulability; avoid causation anchoring.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Karim Bensaid is a 36-year-old right-handed North African man with no significant past medical history who presents to the emergency department with acute-onset left-sided weakness and facial asymmetry. The patient received his first dose of an inactivated COVID-19 vaccine approximately 48 hours prior to presentation. Approximately 24 hours after vaccination, he noticed a tingling and numbness in his left arm and leg while at work. He attributed this to having slept in an awkward position and did not seek medical attention. The tingling persisted through the evening, and he went to bed with it at about 23:00. He also developed a mild bifrontal headache that he treated with paracetamol 1000 mg. The following morning — approximately 48 hours post-vaccination — his wife found him having difficulty getting out of bed. He was unable to move his left arm or leg and the left side of his face was visibly drooping. She also noted he appeared confused and agitated, which was entirely out of character. Emergency medical services were called and he was transported to the emergency department within 45 minutes of symptom recognition. The patient denies any chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, or visual changes. He reports no fever, neck stiffness, rash, or recent illness prior to vaccination. He has no history of migraines, seizures, or prior neurological symptoms. He has no known history of coagulopathy, autoimmune disease, or cardiac disease. There was no recent long-haul travel, immobilization, or surgery. He denies any use of performance-enhancing substances. His wife reports he has been generally healthy and physically active, playing soccer regularly. The family notes a maternal uncle who had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis at age 50, but no family history of stroke or arterial thrombotic events. The temporal relationship between vaccination and symptom onset is noted, though the patient and family are uncertain whether this is coincidental.
